notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Joshua 19:1–26, drawn from the sources searched.

---

## Joshua 19:1–9 — The Inheritance of Simeon

**v. 1: The second lot came out for the clans of the tribe of Simeon. Their inheritance lay within the territory of Judah.**

The "second lot" refers to the second of the seven lots drawn at Shiloh (Benjamin's being the first). Simeon's inheritance falling *within* Judah's territory fulfilled Jacob's prophecy in Genesis 49:7: "I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel." Simeon was the smallest tribe at the last wilderness census (Num 26:14), a likely consequence of the sin at Baal-Peor where a Simeonite prince was a chief offender (Num 25:14). Calvin notes the lot came to Simeon "not as a mark of honor, but rather as a mark of disgrace," yet God had earlier mitigated the parallel curse on Levi by turning it into priestly dignity.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-1.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

**vv. 2–6: Beersheba (or Sheba), Moladah, Hazar-shual, Balah, Ezem, Eltolad, Bethul, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susah, Beth-lebaoth, and Sharuhen—thirteen cities, along with their villages.**

These thirteen cities form the first group and are all situated in the Negeb (the south country). They already appear in Judah's city list (Josh 15:26–32) and again in 1 Chron 4:28–32 with only minor spelling variations. Notable among them: Beersheba, associated with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; Hormah, where Israel had once suffered defeat (Num 14:45) and later gained victory (Num 21:3); and Ziklag, famously given to David by the Philistine king Achish (1 Sam 27:6). Sharuhen is identified by Conder as Tell esh-Sherî'ah, northwest of Beersheba.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-1.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-18-19/

**v. 7: Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan—four cities, along with their villages.**

The second group of four cities. Two lay in the Negeb and two in the Shephelah (lowlands of Judah on the west), indicating Simeon's holdings were not a single compact block but were dispersed. These also appear in Judah's list (Josh 15:32, 42). Ellicott identifies Ain and Rimmon as Timm er-Rumâmîn.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-1.htm

**v. 8: All the villages surrounding these cities as far as Baalath-beer (Ramah of the Negev).**

A summary statement rounding off Simeon's territory. The reference to "Ramah of the Negev" (southern Ramah) distinguishes it from other places named Ramah.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/joshua-19.html

**v. 9: The inheritance of the Simeonites was taken from the territory of Judah, because the share for Judah's descendants was too large for them.**

This verse gives the explicit reason: Judah's portion, assigned at Gilgal from a rough survey, proved on closer inspection to be larger than needed. Justice and brotherly feeling required a modification. Calvin praises Judah's moderation in not contending that the earlier lot (cast "before the LORD") was unalterable — they recognized an honest error had been made in measuring and willingly yielded. Matthew Henry notes: "If a true believer has obtained an unintended and improper advantage in anything, he will give it up without murmuring." Ellicott adds that Judges 1 shows Judah and Simeon cooperating in conquest, illustrating that Joshua's work of allotment left each tribe with work still to do.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-19.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-1.htm (Matthew Henry, Barnes)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

## Joshua 19:10–16 — The Inheritance of Zebulun

**v. 10: The third lot came up for the clans of the tribe of Zebulun. The border of their inheritance stretched as far as Sarid.**

Zebulun, though younger than Issachar, received its lot before Issachar — consistent with the order of Jacob's and Moses' blessings (Gen 49:13; Deut 33:18–19). Sarid (Tell Shadûd) served as the starting-point or centre of the southern boundary.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-19.html (Gill)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

**v. 11: It went up westward to Maralah, reached Dabbesheth, and met the brook east of Jokneam.**

From Sarid the southern boundary ran westward toward the Mediterranean, though not reaching the sea itself (room was left for Asher to interpose). The "brook east of Jokneam" is probably the Kishon River. Jokneam (Tell Keimûn) lay at the southeast end of the Carmel ridge. Calvin notes that here Jacob's prophecy that Zebulun would "dwell by the sea" (Gen 49:13) was fulfilled — the lot gave them the bay of Acre and maritime access. Gill also emphasises this fulfilment.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

**v. 12: From Sarid it turned eastward along the border of Chisloth-tabor and went on to Daberath and up to Japhia.**

The eastern portion of the southern boundary, running from Sarid. Chisloth-tabor (Iksâl), Daberath (Dabûrieh), and Japhia (Yâfa) are all identified places. Daberath was later a Levitical city (Josh 21:28).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

**v. 13: From there it crossed eastward to Gath-hepher and to Eth-kazin; it extended to Rimmon and curved around toward Neah.**

Gath-hepher (El-Mesh-hed) is notable as the birthplace of the prophet Jonah (2 Kings 14:25). Rimmon is identified as Rummâneh, north of Gath-hepher. Several of the minor sites (Eth-kazin, Neah) remain unidentified.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-18-19/

**v. 14: Then the border circled around the north side of Neah to Hannathon and ended at the Valley of Iphtah-el.**

Hannathon (Kefr-'Andn) marks the northeast corner of the boundary. The Valley of Iphtah-el ("God's opening") was likely a gorge running southwest toward the plain.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

**v. 15: Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem. There were twelve cities, along with their villages.**

These cities indicate the western or northwestern extent of Zebulun. Shimron had been a royal Canaanite city whose king Joshua conquered and hanged (Josh 11:1). Bethlehem here is "Bethlehem of Zebulun" — not the Bethlehem of Judah. Judge Ibzan (Judges 12:8–10) came from this northern Bethlehem. Ellicott notes that the name Bethlehem appears only in these two tribes.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-19.html (Gill)

**v. 16: This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Zebulun, including these cities and their villages.**

A closing summary. Though only five cities are explicitly named in the boundary list, the text says "twelve cities." Some named places served as boundary markers rather than towns within Zebulun, and others (like Kartah and Dimnah in Josh 21:34) may have been added later.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-19.html (Gill)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/joshua-19.html

## Joshua 19:17–23 — The Inheritance of Issachar

**v. 17: The fourth lot came out for the clans of the tribe of Issachar.**

Issachar's borders are not traced in detail as Zebulun's were; the description focuses on cities. The tribe's territory occupied the fertile plain of Esdraelon (Jezreel), touching Zebulun and Naphtali on the north, Manasseh on the south and west, and the Jordan on the east.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/joshua-19.html

**v. 18: Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem.**

**Jezreel** (modern Zerin) stood on a steep rocky slope commanding a wide view of the plain. It later became a royal residence of Ahab (1 Kings 21:1) and the scene of Jezebel's death (2 Kings 9:30–37). Hosea refers to the "blood-guiltiness of Jezreel" (Hos 1:4). **Chesulloth** is the same as Chisloth-tabor (v. 12). **Shunem** (Sûlem/Solam), on the western slope of Little Hermon (Mount Duhy), was where the Philistines encamped before Saul's last battle (1 Sam 28:4). It was the home of Abishag (1 Kings 1:3) and the Shunammite woman whose son Elisha raised from the dead (2 Kings 4:8–37). The Shulammite of Song of Songs probably also came from Shunem.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

**v. 19: Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath.**

Hapharaim is possibly the same as Hepher, the residence of a Canaanite king (Josh 12:17), identified by some as modern Afuleh. Shion is not securely identified. Anaharath may be Na'urah on the east side of Little Hermon.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/joshua-19.html

**v. 20: Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez.**

**Kishion** was later a Levitical city (Josh 21:28). In 1 Chron 6:72 (English 6:57) it is erroneously called Kedesh. The sites of Rabbith and Ebez remain unknown.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/joshua-19.html

**v. 21: Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez.**

**Remeth** (or Ramoth/Jarmuth) was a Levitical city (Josh 21:29). **En-gannim** ("garden spring") is modern Jenin, a town noted for its beautiful flowing fountain and abundant gardens — Robinson described it as lying "in the midst of gardens of fruit-trees." Some (e.g., Lightfoot) think Nain, where Jesus raised the widow's son (Luke 7:11), is the same place. En-haddah and Beth-pazzez are unidentified.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-19.html

**v. 22: The border reached Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth-shemesh, and ended at the Jordan. There were sixteen cities, along with their villages.**

**Tabor** here is probably the city on Mount Tabor (not the mountain itself), a Levitical city (1 Chron 6:77) with substantial ancient ruins still visible. **Beth-shemesh** ("house of the sun") was probably a centre of sun-worship, not to be confused with Beth-shemesh in Judah (Josh 15:10) or Naphtali (Josh 19:38). The eastern border ended at the Jordan. Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali had a common border near Tabor.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/joshua-19.html

**v. 23: This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Issachar, including these cities and their villages.**

Summary verse. Ellicott notes an interesting observation: Issachar and Zebulun had been associated with Judah in the same camp during the wilderness march, and their placement in the land next to the house of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh) — with Benjamin between Judah and Joseph — showed "no ordinary wisdom" in cementing the union of all Israel. He further notes that Mary and Joseph of David's line were found dwelling in Nazareth (Zebulun), so "the north and the south alike had 'part in David,' and inheritance in David's Son."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

## Joshua 19:24–26 — The Inheritance of Asher

**v. 24: The fifth lot came out for the clans of the tribe of Asher.**

Asher, descended from Jacob's eighth son by Zilpah (Leah's handmaid), received territory along the Mediterranean coast from Carmel northward to the Phoenician border. Josephus notes the territory included the area around Carmel and the sea.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/joshua-19.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-24.htm

**v. 25: Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph.**

**Helkath** was later a Levitical city (Josh 21:31). It is identified as modern Jerka (or Jelka), a Druse village about three hours east of Acco (Acre). **Hali** is possibly Julis, between Jerka and Akka. **Beten** and **Achshaph** remain uncertain — the Onomasticon places Beten eight Roman miles east of Ptolemais (Acre) but it is not yet found. Achshaph was a royal Canaanite city whose king Joshua defeated (Josh 11:1).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

**v. 26: Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal. On the west the border touched Carmel and Shihor-libnath.**

**Allammelech** is preserved in the name Wady Malek (or Malik), a stream running into the Kishon. **Amad** is conjectured by some to be modern Haifa. **Mishal** (also Mashal, 1 Chron 6:74) was a Levitical city on the coast near Carmel. **Carmel** ("fruit-field") is the famous wooded mountain ridge projecting as a promontory into the sea — celebrated in Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). **Shihor-libnath** is disputed: the name means "black-white" or "muddy river." JFB identifies it with the Nahr Belka (Belus River) below Dor. Keil suggests the Nahr Zerka (possibly Pliny's "crocodile river"), whose name "blue" answers to both *shihor* (black) and *libnath* (white). Calvin notes that the land of Asher was remarkably fertile in corn, fulfilling Jacob's prophecy of Asher's "rich food" (Gen 49:20). Wesley also notes "Carmel by the sea" was a place of eminent fruitfulness, agreeable to the prophecy.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/joshua-19.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

## Summary of Distinctive Protestant Tradition Emphases

**Reformed (Calvin):** Emphasises God's sovereignty in the lot and the fulfilment of prophecy. Sees Simeon's dispersal as divine judgment for ancestral sin (Gen 49:7), while praising Judah's moderation in ceding land. Notes that the surveyors made a human error in over-allocating to Judah and corrected it — evidence that God sometimes leaves his servants "destitute of the spirit of judgment" to keep them humble. On Zebulun, Calvin sees the lot as a "clear confirmation" of Jacob's prophecy "as if God were twice thundering from heaven."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-19.html

**Baptist (Matthew Henry / Spurgeon tradition):** Matthew Henry draws a practical lesson from v. 9: Judah's willingness to give up land teaches that "love seeketh not her own" and that believers who have more than they need should "part with their own to supply what is lacking to their brethren." This reflects a Baptist emphasis on cheerful voluntary sacrifice rather than compulsion.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-1.htm (Matthew Henry)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises the real, tangible nature of God's promises — the detailed place names remind readers that God promised a *real* land. Notes that the land was "divided by casting lots, a method which relied on God to guide the lot," combining "human responsibility (the men's detailed work) and divine direction (trusting God through the lot)." Also stresses that the tribes still had to fight to possess what was given — a picture of believers "possessing their spiritual inheritance" through faith and action.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-18-19/

**Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** Theologically conservative, emphasising the precise fulfilment of prophecy. Notes the apparent contradiction that Simeon's cities appear in two groups in both Negeb and Shephelah — which "overthrows" the idea that Simeon received a single connected territory. Emphasises that the situation of many towns is still unknown, cautioning against over-confident identification.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/19-1.htm (Keil)

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Provides detailed geographical identification using Conder's Survey of Western Palestine, bridging traditional commentary with 19th-century archaeological findings. Ellicott traces the fulfilment of Jacob's words through Israel's later history, noting that Simeon's dispersal was compounded when the tribe, though adhering to the northern kingdom after Solomon, was geographically cut off from it by the whole breadth of Judah.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-19.html

---

*Note: No distinct Catholic, Orthodox, or modern critical-scholarly perspectives on these specific verses were found within the searchable sources. The geographical listings in Joshua 19 are among the least disputed passages, and commentary traditions tend to converge on the same basic facts of identification, fulfilment of patriarchal prophecies, and the theme of God's faithful provision.*
